title: State Hoisting Finally Clicked For Me
excerpt: A stateless composable isn't a limitation — it's the whole point. Notes from the week I stopped fighting Compose's state model.
bodyMarkdown:
I kept writing composables that owned their own `remember { mutableStateOf(...) } ` and then wondering why my preview and my real screen drifted apart. The fix was smaller than I expected: pull the state up, pass it down as parameters, and pass the *events* back up as lambdas.

> A composable that reads and writes its own state is a composable you can't reuse anywhere else.

Once a component only takes `value` and `onValueChange`, it stops caring who owns the truth. The parent can back it with a `ViewModel`, a `SavedStateHandle`, a plain `remember`, or a fake for a preview — the composable itself doesn't know or care.

## The pattern in practice

```kotlin
@Composable
fun Counter(count: Int, onIncrement: () -> Unit) {
    Button(onClick = onIncrement) {
        Text("Count: $count")
    }
}
```

No `remember` inside `Counter` at all. The caller decides where `count` actually lives:

```kotlin
var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
Counter(count = count, onIncrement = { count++ })
```

That's it. That's the whole trick, and it's also exactly why `TextField(value, onValueChange)` is shaped the way it is — it was hoisted state all along, I just hadn't named it yet.

## Why this matters beyond tidiness

Hoisting isn't just a style preference — it's what makes state *testable* and *previewable*. A stateless composable can be dropped into a `@Preview` with a hardcoded value and no ViewModel wiring. A stateful one drags its dependencies with it everywhere it goes.

The rule of thumb I'm using now: state should live at the lowest common ancestor of everything that reads or writes it, and no lower. If only one composable touches it, keep it local. The moment a sibling needs to react to it too, hoist it up until it does.
